title: The Theory of Polycrisis Resilience
subtitle: Toward a Unified Framework for Human and Systemic Vulnerability Reduction
description: A foundational theoretical publication explaining how human societies, economies, and interconnected systems can systematically reduce their vulnerability to…
contribution: Establishes the formal theoretical architecture of Polycrisis Resilience: connecting six integrated disciplines, answering one central and six supporting research questions, and investigating six proposed foundational dimensions linking interconnected risks to human and systemic vulnerability reduction.
abstract:
The Theory of Polycrisis Resilience serves as a foundational theoretical publication within the H Heuristics Polycrisis Resilience Research Series, building on the flagship framework originated by Hunter Hughes (https://researchreports.hheuristics.com/reports/polycrisis-resilience-flagship-report/).
Its primary purpose is to develop a coherent theoretical explanation of how human societies, economies, and interconnected systems can systematically reduce their vulnerability to multiple, interacting, and compounding global risks—uniting polycrisis theory, development economics, sustainable convergence, technology diffusion, human and institutional development, and prevention economics into a single testable framework.

keyFindings.title: Resilience should not be understood exclusively as the capacity to withstand or recover from crises, but also as the capacity to systematically reduce the underlying structural conditions that generate vulnerability to interconnected global risks.

When structural vulnerability is high across exposure, sensitivity, development deficits, and adaptive gaps, an 18.0% primary climate shock cascades across grids, food, health, fiscal, and institutional systems to produce a 61.0% compounded systemic impact.

The H Heuristics theoretical model proposes six foundational dimensions—economic development, technological diffusion, environmental sustainability, human development, institutional capacity, and infrastructure resilience—exhibiting positive cross-dimensional correlations (r = 0.68–0.86) while remaining an open, empirically testable taxonomy rather than a closed dogma.

Integrating development economics, sustainable convergence, technology diffusion, and prevention economics shifts capital allocation from low-return reactive bailouts (1.3x–1.8x social BCR) to high-return ex-ante vulnerability reduction (6.8x–11.0x social BCR).
